title: Binary Trees (Conceptual)
tagline: Binary tree concepts: root, leaf, subtree, sibling, depth, height, inorder/preorder/postorder traversals, binary search trees and tree shape.

The syllabus topic list was taken from the verified 2027 syllabus; the explanations, examples and questions here are original and were not taken from any board examination paper, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: A binary tree is a branching data structure in which each node has at most two children. This chapter explains the basic vocabulary of trees, including root, leaf, subtree, sibling, depth, height and level, and it describes the three common traversals: inorder, preorder and postorder. It also introduces binary search trees as a special ordered kind of binary tree and discusses why the shape of a tree matters for efficiency.

blocks.text: A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children. By convention those children are called the left child and the right child. That simple restriction is what makes a binary tree a binary tree. A tree with no such restriction can have many children per node; a binary tree limits each node to zero, one or two children. That limit is what gives binary trees their shape and their usefulness.

One node is the root. The root is the topmost node of the tree and the starting point for reaching every other node. Except for the root, every node has exactly one parent, which is the node above it. A node with no children is called a leaf. A node that is not a leaf is sometimes called an internal node. These terms are not just vocabulary; they are the basic way of talking about any tree.

learn.title: Key terms: subtree, sibling, depth, height, level

blocks.text: A subtree is a node together with all of its descendants. Every node in a binary tree is itself the root of a smaller binary tree. That is one reason trees are useful: they are recursive by nature, because the same idea reappears at every level. A subtree is usually named after the node at its root, so you can talk about the left subtree of a node or the right subtree of a node.

Nodes that share the same parent are called siblings. The depth or level of a node is how far it is from the root. The height of a tree is a measure of how tall it is, often defined by the longest path from the root to a leaf. These ideas are about position and shape rather than stored values. They matter because the shape of a tree affects how efficiently you can work with it.

If the longest path from root to leaf has two edges, the tree height is often described as 2; a node on that path has a depth equal to its distance from the root.

blocks.text: Traversal means visiting every node in a tree in some order. For a binary tree, the three usual depth-first traversals are inorder, preorder and postorder. Each one visits the node and its subtrees in a different sequence. In inorder, you traverse the left subtree, visit the node, then traverse the right subtree. In preorder, you visit the node first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. In postorder, you traverse the left subtree, then the right subtree, then visit the node.

The difference between these orders matters because each order is useful in different situations. Inorder is often used when you want to visit values in sorted order from a binary search tree. Preorder is useful when you want to process a node before its subtrees. Postorder is useful when you need to process the subtrees before the node, for example when deleting or computing something from subtrees upward. You do not need to memorise a code template perfectly; you need to know what order each traversal visits nodes in.

learn.title: Binary search trees: a special case with ordering

blocks.text: A binary search tree is a binary tree with an extra rule about ordering. For each node, the values in its left subtree are usually considered smaller, and the values in its right subtree are usually considered larger. That rule is what makes searching in a binary search tree efficient in the average case, because you can discard half the remaining tree at each step by comparing with the current node.

A binary search tree is still a binary tree, but not every binary tree is a binary search tree. The syllabus treats binary trees at a conceptual level, so you should be able to explain the difference: the shape is still binary, but the values are arranged with the search property in mind. That search property is also why inorder traversal of a binary search tree gives values in order.

blocks.text: The shape of a binary tree is as important as its contents. A tree can be tall and skinny or short and broad. A complete binary tree packs nodes neatly, level by level, so that the shape is as compact as possible for the number of nodes. A balanced tree keeps the height small so that operations stay efficient. These ideas are conceptual at this stage, but they matter because a tree that is badly shaped can be much slower to search than one that is well shaped.

Height is a measure of how many levels a tree has, or how far the deepest leaf is from the root. A tree with small height is generally better for search, insertion and deletion, because fewer levels means fewer steps in the worst case. That is why balancing and completeness are discussed alongside binary trees: they are about keeping the tree useful rather than just logically correct.

blocks.text: Binary trees are useful when data has a natural hierarchy. A file system, an expression tree, a family tree and a decision process can all be modelled as trees. A binary tree is especially useful when each decision point has at most two choices, or when the data can be arranged so that smaller and larger values fall to the left and right. That is the kind of situation where a binary tree is a better fit than a flat list.

Binary trees also connect to the idea of efficient search. If the tree is arranged as a binary search tree, searching can be much faster than scanning a list from end to end. That is why binary trees are often taught alongside searching and sorting ideas. The syllabus keeps the treatment conceptual, so the focus is on understanding what a tree is, what traversals do, and why the shape matters, not on implementing every variant.

learn.title: Binary tree versus other data structures

blocks.text: A binary tree is not just another list. A list is linear: each element has at most one successor. A binary tree is branching: each node can have two successors. That means a tree can represent relationships that a list cannot represent naturally, especially hierarchy. The trade-off is that trees are more complex to traverse and reason about than a flat list.

Compared with a stack or a queue, a binary tree is much more flexible but also more complex. A stack and a queue impose a strict access order, while a tree allows many different orders through traversal. That flexibility is useful, but it also means you have to be clear about which order you want and why. The syllabus expects you to be able to compare these structures, not just to name them.
